title: Accurate Self-Attention Wavefunctions at Large Scale
authors: Filippo Gaggioli, Sam Azadi, Liang Fu
abstract: Self-attention neural networks provide powerful variational wavefunctions that surpass the expressivity of traditional variational ansatze. This expressivity, however, comes with increased computational complexity, raising a pressing question about scalability -- can such wavefunctions retain their accuracy at large system sizes? We apply self-attention wavefunctions to the two-dimensional homogeneous electron gas for up to N=169 particles, obtaining energies systematically lower than state-of-the-art DMC. Direct access to the ground state wavefunction further lets us recover the full collective-mode dispersion of the liquid phase, from the small-q plasmon branch to a roton-like minimum near q=2k_F. Observables at N=91 and N=169 are in near-perfect agreement, indicating convergence to the thermodynamic limit.
summary: The authors demonstrate that self-attention neural networks can generate highly accurate variational wavefunctions for the 2D homogeneous electron gas. By applying this method to large systems (up to N=169), they achieve energies competitive with state-of-the-art DMC and accurately recover complex collective excitations like plasmons and rotons, proving scalability.
main_problem: The primary challenge is determining if self-attention wavefunctions can maintain high accuracy and scalability when applied to large quantum systems, surpassing traditional variational ansatze.
main_result: The method successfully yields systematically lower energies than state-of-the-art DMC for up to 169 particles in the 2D HEG, demonstrating convergence towards the thermodynamic limit.
method: Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) is employed using a self-attention neural network architecture to generate highly expressive variational wavefunctions ($\psi_	heta$).
model_or_system: The study models the two-dimensional homogeneous electron gas (HEG) of spin-polarized electrons, governed by a standard Coulomb interaction Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Ground state energy ($E$), momentum distribution $n(\mathbf{k})$, static structure factor $S(q)$, and collective mode dispersion $\epsilon(q)$.
important_parameters: System sizes up to $N=169$ particles, interaction strength controlled by the dimensionless density parameter $r_s$ (e.g., $r_s=30$ or $r_s=40$).
main_assumptions: The wavefunction is constructed as an antisymmetric fermionic determinant using generalized orbitals derived from the self-attention mechanism.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the self-attention architecture, momentum occupation $n(k)$ showing metallic behavior, and structure factor $S(q)$ revealing plasmon and roton features in the liquid phase.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the self-attention approach for wavefunctions, applies it to the HEG Hamiltonian, calculates ground state energies via VMC, and then analyzes correlated observables like $S(q)$ and $\epsilon(q)$ across varying system sizes to prove convergence.
why_interesting: This work pushes the boundary of computational quantum chemistry by applying advanced machine learning techniques (self-attention) to solve fundamental problems in strongly correlated electron systems, offering a scalable alternative to traditional high-accuracy methods like DMC.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Self-attention neural network and VMC: Illus- tration of our self-attention architecture (left), and its role inside the VMC algorithm (right).

FIG. 2. Momentum space occupation and structure factor. Left panels: for rs = 30, the system displays metallic behavior, as signaled by the sharp Fermi surface discontinuity in the momentum space occupations n(k). Right panels: for rs = 40, the electrons form a crystalline state (see the density snapshot in the inset). Correspondingly, prominent Bragg peaks appear in the structure factor S(q).

FIG. 3. Collective modes (rs = 30): the energy q2/S(q) provides a variational upper bound on the dispersion of the collective modes for the HEG ground state. The plasmon branch ∝√q at small q evolves into a roton-like minimum around 2kF associated to the incipient crystalline order. The quantitative agreement across system sizes certifies accuracy in approaching the thermodynamic limit.
